standard_or_claim: Qin-certified measures carried a forty-character First Emperor inscription; a sixty-character Second Emperor supplement was later added.
observed_practice: A pre-unification bronze scoop from the Qin palace treasury was certified in 221 BCE, then re-inscribed and supplemented in 209 BCE. Its earlier use-labels remained visible.
sample_label: one excavated scoop plus parallel inscribed objects
interpretation: Standardization could reuse and certify an existing object rather than replace every object at once.
limits: One richly documented scoop is not a census of measures or proof of exact conformity throughout the empire; its 980 ml capacity is an object measurement, not a universal conversion model.

standard_or_claim: Later Han accounts attributed a sudden unification of writing to the First Emperor; Qin small-seal script served official epigraphic purposes.
observed_practice: Pre- and post-unification epigraphy does not show one sudden comprehensive shift; even government edict plates are not written in a completely uniform hand.
interpretation: An official written norm could improve recognition and copying without instantly erasing regional or scribal variation.
limits: This comparison concerns written forms rather than spoken-language unification and does not assign a literacy rate or a script-uniformity score.

standard_or_claim: A common Qin document-tablet length was about 23 cm.
observed_practice: All twenty-five complete upward reports in Staack's Liye sample fall within ±0.5 cm of 23 cm.
interpretation: Length may have been operationally important for transport or storage, so local producers followed it closely.
limits: The transport or container explanation is plausible but unproven because only container labels survive; the twenty-five reports are one bounded Qianling sample.

standard_or_claim: An ordinance prescribed tablet widths by the number of text columns and tolerated deviations only up to 0.23 cm.
observed_practice: None of the twenty-five Liye reports stayed within the legal width tolerance; narrower tablets saved wood and production effort.
interpretation: A rule could remain legible to administrators even when local resource constraints made literal compliance impractical.
limits: The evidence does not show whether fines were imposed or waived, nor whether other counties followed the width rule more closely.

standard_or_claim: An ordinance limited a roughly 23 cm tablet to no more than twenty-two characters per column.
observed_practice: Fourteen of the twenty-five complete Liye reports exceed the character limit; no clear change through time or office explains the breaches.
interpretation: Officials preserved usable documents while compressing text when material, time, and staffing constraints pressed.
limits: The eleven conforming count is the complement of fourteen reported breaches; this does not establish that every line on each document was equally regulated.

standard_or_claim: Grain-disbursal records followed prescribed content categories: store, amount, date, officials, recipients, supervision, and handling.
observed_practice: All twenty-two complete Liye tallies were fairly standardized in content, but only sixteen used the dominant layout A; six used A2, B, or C arrangements accepted in practice.
interpretation: Standardized fields made transactions comparable while scribes retained leeway over the physical arrangement of those fields.
limits: Layout A is the observed dominant layout and closest to the statutory sequence; the ordinance did not necessarily require this exact visual layout.
